What is the most promising propulsion technology for theoretical manned Interstellar travel? What percentage of the speed of light could be theoretically reached? Good questions, and ones that require serious qualifications. The answer to the first question is, we don’t know! The vast distances of interstellar space, the challenges of generating and maintaining enormous amounts of energy, the difficulty of shielding a spaceship and its crew from cosmic radiation, the issue of accelerating and decelerating a spaceship, and the time it takes to get anywhere once you’re underway are all hurdles that need to be overcome. If you relax some of these constraints, there are several contenders. First, and most likely, using a fusion reactor. By fusing hydrogen atoms into helium, a spaceship could use the energy released to propel itself forward. The problem is, we don’t have a working fusion reactor yet, despite decades of trying, and even if we did, the energy output might not be enough. The advantage of fusion is that it provides a relatively high exhaust velocity (the speed at which the propellant is ejected from the spaceship). Then there are Bussard ramjets, which essentially collect the interstellar medium (mostly hydrogen) in front of the spaceship and use that for fusion. The problem here is that the density of the interstellar medium is very low, so you’d need an enormous collection device. Next, there are the ideas around antimatter, specifically employing a matter-antimatter reaction to generate energy. This would lead to incredibly high exhaust velocities, but the challenge is the extreme difficulty of producing, storing, and containing antimatter. Finally, there’s the possibility of a “warp drive”, bending spacetime around the spaceship. This would in principle enable faster-than-light travel without violating the laws of physics, but the energy requirements are almost certainly beyond anything we could generate. And then, there’s the issue of the unknown: perhaps some breakthrough is possible that we haven't even considered yet. As for the percentage of the speed of light that could be reached: again, it depends. With fusion, one could reasonably aim for 10% of the speed of light. With antimatter, perhaps 30% or even faster, but the technological hurdles are enormous. The more exotic proposals, like warp drives, could, in principle, reach any speed, but the energy requirements would be prohibitive. Overall, there is no proven technology and no real consensus. The best we can say is that with our current knowledge, interstellar travel remains firmly in the realm of science fiction. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

I always read Victor Toth that the singularity is a moment in the future, not a point in place. What will happen to an observer falling into a black hole as he sees it for himself? Will he be crushed? The singularity is indeed a temporal event, a future boundary of spacetime, not a localized spatial position that one might somehow "reach." But as to what happens to an unfortunate soul plummeting into a black hole, the answer is a resounding yes, though perhaps "pulverized" is a more accurate descriptor than "crushed." As the hapless observer nears the singularity, the relentless tidal forces, born from the extreme gravitational gradient, become utterly insurmountable. The observer's body will be stretched and squeezed with increasing ferocity, a process often referred to as "spaghettification". This is not a gradual descent into a comfortable oblivion. The observer’s demise will be quite a swift one. The gravitational pull on his feet, for instance, will be astronomically greater than on his head, resulting in an elongation that rapidly escalates. Similarly, the observer will also be compressed laterally. The poor observer's atoms will be ripped apart, overcome by the very forces of gravity that had initially drawn him in. This spaghettification, this relentless stretching and tearing, is what ultimately awaits any infalling object, including light itself, that crosses the event horizon of a black hole. The entire process, from crossing the horizon to the final, atomic disintegration, transpires shockingly quickly, dependent on the size of the black hole. In particular, for the supermassive black holes that are thought to reside at the centers of galaxies, spaghettification is more gradual. In any case, the observer's existence, as we understand it, comes to an abrupt end. Whether the observer experiences this process consciously is a matter of debate and conjecture, but it is beyond doubt that that observer will simply cease to exist. Why is it challenging to comprehend quantum mechanics? Can we simply accept Einstein's perspective on reality instead of the concept of uncertainty? The short answer is no, we cannot. This is because whether we like it or not, quantum mechanics is experimentally confirmed down to the finest details. The way reality works, at least at its most fundamental level, happens to be quantum mechanical, and quantum mechanics is counterintuitive. Indeed, the very reason why quantum mechanics is difficult to comprehend is that it goes against our intuitions. Our intuitions, after all, are honed in our experience with the macroscopic world. This is a world in which any uncertainty is either negligible or a mere artifact of our ignorance. And the macroscopic world, of course, is all that we know directly through our senses. We can easily toss a ball and predict where it will land, or estimate how far a car will travel in an hour. So we develop intuitions that, in effect, assume that the position and momentum of objects are always well-defined at all times. This is simply not the case at the subatomic level. There, particles do not, in fact, have well-defined positions and velocities. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle formalizes this: the better the measurement of position, the less well-defined the momentum will be, and vice versa. It's not the imperfections of our measurement apparatus, though. The uncertainty is intrinsic to the fundamental nature of reality itself. Einstein, for all of his monumental achievements, was wrong about this one. "God does not play dice" he stated, and he never accepted the probabilistic nature of quantum mechanics. As many other physicists who were equally unconvinced by the strangeness of this new theory, he preferred to believe that there was an underlying deeper, hidden reality that would restore our familiar notion of causality. But all experiments continue to prove him wrong, and continue to support the notion that "God does play dice". Not only that, a century after quantum mechanics was formalized during the “heroic age” of physics, we still do not have a good way of interpreting it. We still argue over what quantum mechanics actually *means*, and in what sense it may be considered a “complete” theory. There is a rather bizarre “measurement problem”, which continues to preoccupy physicists. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Can antimatter be considered as "visible matter" because it can interact with light even though it has the opposite charge of normal matter? That's certainly one way to look at it. Ultimately, "visible matter" isn't really a scientific term. I mean, we don't have a standardized definition or threshold. It's more like a colloquialism. We often use it to refer to the stuff that, well, we *see*. And what do we see? Primarily, stuff that interacts with photons, i.e., light. So, if antimatter interacts with light, does it count as "visible"? You could argue yes. In fact, you could argue even more forcefully that antimatter is *more* "visible" than, say, dark matter, which, as far as we know, doesn't interact with light at all. Moreover, the interaction between antimatter and light is, in some ways, even more dramatic than the interaction between light and ordinary matter. When antimatter interacts with ordinary matter, the result is annihilation, a complete conversion into energy, usually in the form of photons. This is pretty darn visible, wouldn't you say? Think of it like a miniature Big Bang, albeit one that's exceedingly brief and localized. Now, of course, antimatter is also invisible in the sense that it is not directly visible by itself, not the way that everyday objects are. But that's true of most things we perceive. The vast majority of what we think is an object is actually just empty space between fundamental particles, for instance. Photons are also invisible until they interact with something. So, to summarize, antimatter *can* be considered "visible matter" in the sense that it interacts with light in a way that can be observed. In fact, one could argue that the evidence for antimatter is its interaction with light, its annihilation and creation of photons. Pretty cool, huh? If a human somehow managed to travel to the Sagittarius A* black hole, would they see exactly what the 2022 image shows us? No, not exactly. While the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) collaboration’s composite image of Sagittarius A* – the supermassive black hole at the center of our galaxy – is stunning, that is a snapshot, a freeze-frame, of sorts. It captures a specific moment in time, a carefully curated average of all the light that the EHT array, operating at a wavelength of 1.3 mm, could gather during a given observing run. Moreover, it’s a composite. The EHT hasn’t actually “seen” anything: it has only observed the faint radio waves emanating from the vicinity of the black hole. The published image is an educated guess, a sophisticated reconstruction based on complex modeling and data processing. So, if you were to somehow find yourself orbiting Sagittarius A*, the view would be dynamically ever-changing. The radio waves we are seeing would shift. The accretion disk surrounding the black hole would be a furious, ever-shifting ballet of hot gas spiraling inward. The actual amount of light reaching your eyes, even if you had the ability to see the light, would also depend on your exact location, and on the interplay of the light with the gravitational field. Indeed, given the extreme gravity, light paths would be bent, twisted, and distorted, giving rise to effects such as gravitational lensing and relativistic beaming. In fact, the image of the black hole would appear smeared, warped, and subject to continual distortion, not the refined, almost perfect, image from the EHT. Dear Viktor Toth, with respect to your answer on the expression of the weak force, could you please correct the second equation? The first one for V(r) is right, but the second seems to have a typo, so that it is not displayed. Certainly. I've reviewed the answer, and you are correct. The second equation did have a typographical error, causing it to be omitted from the display. I've attempted to rectify this. The corrected expression for A(r) should read thusly: A(r) = ( g / 4 π r ) exp ( -m r ) . This represents the vector potential associated with the weak interaction, and it is, of course, fundamentally different from the gravitational potential (which has no exponential factor, as the force carrier, the graviton, has no mass). However, the essential point pertains to their shared characteristic: both forces exhibit a 1/r behavior at small distances (i.e., when r approaches zero), which is to say, they grow in strength as the distance between the interacting particles decreases. This behavior is a defining trait of “long-range” forces. The exponential term, however, indicates that the weak force differs from gravity: its strength diminishes rapidly as the distance between the interacting particles increases and becomes essentially negligible at larger distances. This “short-range” characteristic is, in fact, dependent on the mass m of the weak interaction force carriers, the W and Z bosons. This mass is relatively large, which results in the weak force being short-ranged. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

How is the speed of light considered constant in all frames despite the effects of gravitational and inertial time dilation? That’s a tricky one, isn't it? Let's consider this meticulously. The speed of light, denoted by *c*, is not just a speed; it’s more fundamentally a universal constant. It's so fundamental, in fact, that our entire understanding of space and time is built upon it. Einstein’s special relativity, the foundation upon which our current understanding of spacetime stands, is built, in essence, on this single, fundamental postulate: The speed of light in a vacuum is constant for all observers, regardless of the motion of the light source. But what about gravity and inertia, which by all accounts, do affect time? Isn't that a paradox? Not quite. It is true that general relativity tells us that time dilates in the presence of both gravity and acceleration (i.e., inertia). A clock in a stronger gravitational field ticks slower, and a clock accelerating at a constant rate will also tick slower relative to an inertial observer. The problem, however, is the way we define “speed”. Speed itself is simply distance divided by time. So if time itself is affected by gravity and inertia, then it follows that the measurement of distance, which would involve sending light signals back and forth, would also necessarily be affected; and it would have to be, in such a way that the ratio of the two remains the same. Imagine two observers, one in a strong gravitational field and the other far away from any gravitational influence. Both would have their own reliable clocks, but the clock in the gravitational field would tick slower. However, the speed of light as measured by both observers would be the same. The observer in the gravitational field would find that distances as well are shorter compared to the “far away" observer. And vice versa, the far-away observer would measure both time and distances to appear distorted. When we say “the speed of light is constant”, what we are really saying is that the ratio of distance to time, as measured locally by an observer, is constant. It is a property of spacetime itself, not of light. Light simply travels within the rules imposed by spacetime. Thus, it isn’t some weird accident that the speed of light is constant, but a consequence of the structure of the universe. Indeed, it is the very foundation for how the universe works, at least, as far as we can measure. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

What are tensors (as used in special/general relativity) exactly? Tensors are just a mathematical construct. A very useful one, at that. They can be defined in many ways, depending on what one is trying to do. But for our purpose, they're best understood as a generalization of vectors and matrices. A vector is something with a magnitude and a direction, and a matrix is a table, a two-dimensional array. A tensor is a multi-dimensional array. The simplest tensors are scalars, which can be thought of as 0-dimensional arrays (just a single number), and vectors, which can be thought of as 1-dimensional arrays (a list of numbers representing the components of the vector in a particular coordinate system). Matrices are 2-dimensional arrays, and then there are 3-dimensional and 4-dimensional etc. arrays, which are higher-rank tensors. Every time one does coordinate transformations, the components of the tensor change in a predictable way. It is this very property that makes tensors so useful for describing physical phenomena in curved spacetime. A tensor equation is something like “the stress-energy tensor equals something else”. Here, the objects on both sides of the equation will look different depending on which coordinate system you choose, but the equation itself remains valid. This is why tensors are so well-suited for describing physical laws: they provide a coordinate-independent way of expressing relationships between physical quantities. In general relativity, tensors are used to describe the curvature of spacetime, the distribution of energy and momentum, and the gravitational field. They are absolutely essential for understanding how gravity works, and how it affects the universe. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Can a black hole at its center be destroyed? If so, what would be the method to do so? Would the intense gravity make it impossible to escape and cause any damage? Theoretically, yes, a black hole's singularity, the very core as we understand it, could be considered "destroyed". But let us first recognize that “destroyed” is not a well-defined concept when applied to black holes: what we truly perceive as a black hole depends on the outside perspective. In the context of general relativity, the black hole itself is not some object floating in space, but the result of a distortion of spacetime. Any attempt to "destroy" this distortion would, in effect, require reversing the process that created it, and even then, the effects of the distortion may remain in some form. This means that any actual "destruction" of the singularity, or perhaps the complete evaporation of the black hole, would necessitate an influence acting upon the singularity itself. So how to achieve this? We can only speculate. One possible means is if the black hole were to "die" or "evaporate," as predicted by the theory of Hawking radiation. In this scenario, the black hole would gradually leak particles due to quantum effects, ultimately diminishing in mass and, theoretically, disappearing completely. If the black hole is small enough, at the end of its lifetime, it could simply vanish. No "intense gravity" would prevent this process: indeed, Hawking radiation is precisely a symptom of the most intense gravity. Moreover, it is the intense gravity that makes this evaporation possible. Another theoretical approach, invoking quantum gravity, could involve causing the singularity to “tunnel,” that is, to transform itself into something else to which it is connected by highly curved spacetime. There are several theoretical models of quantum gravity, yet we cannot pinpoint what would happen in that scenario. We still don't have experimental support for it. But at the very least, intense gravity would not prevent destruction. We just don't know how to bring it about yet. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

What is the definition of observation in the double-slit interference experiment of light? Can the visual observation of intelligent creatures determine whether light is a particle or a wave? It's a tricky question, isn't it? The very act of "observation" in this context, and particularly in this famous experiment, alters the outcome. Let's unravel this perplexing conundrum. Observation, in the quantum realm, isn't merely a passive act of seeing; it's an active interaction. When we observe, we're not simply bearing witness; we're intervening. To observe a photon, one has to interact with it. That interaction, like using a measuring device to pin down a photon's trajectory, essentially “forces” the photon to behave like a particle. It "collapses" the wave function. Before observation, light exists as a wave and passes through both slits, creating the interference pattern that demonstrates wave-like behavior. But when observation is attempted, the measurement device—a camera, a detector—interacts with the photons, forcing them (or at least making it highly probable) to pass through only one slit. This is how we determine its position and trajectory, not its wave-like properties. The moment we try to determine “which slit”, the interference pattern disappears, and the photons behave like particles, creating a simple distribution on a screen behind the slits. The interference pattern, the unmistakable signature of a wave, vanishes the moment we attempt to "observe" which path they take. One has to be extraordinarily careful how we interpret this. This does not preclude the possibility that a living creature may, in principle, constitute a measuring device. A conscious being, with the ability to perceive, process, and record information about the photons, could indeed be considered an observer. But it doesn’t change much, if anything, in the experiment. I doubt a conscious observer of light could determine its nature any better than an inanimate one. Again, the fundamental issue isn't about the nature of the observer. It's about the interaction. The key is *how* we observe, how we measure the photons’ position. It is this experimental setup that determines whether the light behaves like a wave or a particle. If we are measuring its interaction, it behaves like a particle. If we are not, it behaves like a wave. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Is it a coincidence that all particles with Higgs mass carry electric charges? No, that is not a coincidence. The Standard Model of particle physics dictates a profound connection between mass and electric charge, particularly regarding the Higgs mechanism. In fact, the Higgs field couples to the electric charge of a particle, so it's not that a particle *has* electric charge and *then* acquires mass. It's that the very mechanism by which particles acquire mass, through interaction with the Higgs field, is inextricably linked to their electric charge. The stronger the coupling to the Higgs field, the greater the mass. But even in the most complex models, there are particles without electric charge, but they still interact with the Higgs. The reason is that the Higgs field does not interact with all particles in the same way. For example, quarks and leptons – fundamental particles of matter – acquire mass through the Higgs mechanism, but this coupling is *proportional* to their electric charge. The Higgs field also interacts with itself, which gives rise to the mass of the Higgs boson. It also interacts with other bosons that transfer the forces. So no mass without coupling. No way. Why are the negative energy solutions to Dirac equation interpreted as antimatters instead of virtual matters? Ah, the million-dollar question, isn't it? The Dirac equation, a cornerstone of relativistic quantum mechanics, predicts the existence of antiparticles with uncanny accuracy. But the initial interpretation of its negative energy solutions as "negative energy particles" turned out to be a mathematical dead end, not to mention a physically bizarre one. The problem? They’d behave in ways that violate all the known laws of physics, including the one that governs their energy: They would have a tendency to cascade down, radiating an infinite amount of energy as they did. In addition, the state of the vacuum would have been inherently unstable and subject to various kinds of infinities, which is never good in theoretical physics. Now, as for the “virtual matter” idea, it's not entirely wrong, but it's also not the final answer. Virtual particles are, indeed, a crucial concept in quantum field theory. They are the transient fluctuations of the quantum fields that mediate interactions between matter (as we currently understand “matter”) and, as such, they are a crucial component of all known forces of nature. However they pop into existence for only a fleeting moment. These virtual particles, by their very nature, do not obey Einstein’s famous mass-energy relation. However, the negative energy solutions of Dirac’s equation cannot be interpreted as such since they are, in fact, a solution to Einstein’s equations... and thus, obey the laws of relativity. The answer lies in something more profound, a completely different approach which is the cornerstone of modern quantum field theory. Rather than interpreting these negative energy solutions as describing "negative energy particles", Dirac realized that one could interpret them as the absence of positive-energy particles. This is a sea of negative energy states, that is, mostly filled but with occasional "holes.” Any time a negative energy electron is absent, it will appear as a positive charge. And since every single element has an equal amount of electrons and their corresponding protons, they will never be negative with each other, but zero. So rather than “electrons” with negative energies, there would be “holes” with positive energies, and positive charges. These holes are what we call antielectrons, otherwise known as *positrons*, the antimatter counterparts of electrons. This idea, the “Dirac sea,” was a real leap of genius. It paved the way for our modern understanding of antimatter, particles with the same mass but opposite charge and other quantum numbers. The Dirac equation isn't just a mathematical curiosity; it's a profound statement about the underlying symmetry of the universe and the intimate connection between matter and antimatter. In 3 dimensions, Cartesian coordinate systems are distinguishable from their mirror images. What is the situation in 3+1 dimensions and how many inequivalent images are there? Yes, in 3+1 dimensions, even with the three spatial dimensions and one time dimension, the concept of "handedness" still matters. We can construct a coordinate system in spacetime, and it is possible to make such a coordinate system be either "left-handed" or "right-handed", just like in 3 dimensions. But this time, the question of “mirror images” is much more subtle, and the answer hinges on a crucial understanding: the “mirror image” of a spacetime coordinate system is not just a simple spatial inversion, as one might intuitively expect. We must also consider time reversal. Specifically, the operation of mirroring a coordinate system in 3+1 dimensions consists of two actions: first, inverting all of the spatial coordinates, and second, reversing the direction of time. Mathematically, this can be written as : (t, x, y, z) → (-t, -x, -y, -z)The question now becomes, how many inequivalent such systems are there? Well, just like in 3 dimensions, the spatial inversion (e.g., flipping your hand from left to right) transforms a right-handed coordinate system into a left-handed one and vice versa. But time reversal? Time reversal does not change the handedness of a coordinate system. Why is that? Because time is orthogonal to the three spatial dimensions. But here’s the catch: the laws of physics are, in general, not symmetrical under time reversal. What does this mean in practice? It essentially means that when you reverse the direction of time, you can observe a phenomenon that would not be possible when time runs forward. Here is a good example from quantum mechanics: when an unstable elementary particle decays, it often does so by emitting other particles. If you were to reverse time, this process would not occur; it *cannot* occur. Therefore, the operation of time reversal does change the fundamental character of physical reality. It would seem that as in the 3-dimensional case, at a bare minimum, we have at least two inequivalent systems in 3+1 dimensions: right-handed and left-handed. However, the laws of physics may, or may not, be symmetric under time reversal. If they are symmetric, then the left-handed system mirrors the right-handed one; that is, it would be indistinguishable from the original. If not, in many cases, the physics would not be unchanged. Then we would be in a situation in which there were four inequivalent systems: right-handed, left-handed, right-handed but time-reversed, and left-handed but time-reversed. Note, however: if only the "weak force" is active (i.e., time-reversal symmetry is violated, but all other symmetries are upheld), only two systems remain. It might be said that we cannot tell if this is the case. The weak force is “weak” because it only applies to very small particles: neutrinos, and other light particles. And their behavior is well understood. This makes the determination of what types of systems, and how many exist, a matter of what symmetries are preserved. When the particle is being observed, does its wave function collapse into a size less point, or a very small Gaussian packet? That's a good question. It touches upon the very heart of the measurement problem in quantum mechanics. The short answer is, well, neither, or both, depending on how you look at it. But before I get into the details, allow me to address a common misconception. People often picture the "collapse" of the wave function as a physical process that occurs instantaneously, akin to a magical shrinking of the particle. This is not quite right. It’s more of a change in our *knowledge* of the system, rather than an actual physical shrinking of the particle itself. Consider this: until we measure a particle’s position, we only know its *probability* distribution, described by its wave function. Thus, before a measurement, its position truly is not defined. After we have measured it, we *know* the particle has been located to a certain point! We still cannot say that this point is “smaller” than the original wave function (as it is the case with the collapse) or more precisely, we will never be able to tell even if one day we’ll figure out how to measure the position of any particle without distorting the value of the position itself. If we were to perform the same measurements several times, we might notice that each measurement yields a slightly different position. However, if we were to repeat the measurement a vast number of times, it would be seen that the positions are somewhat similar, for example, concentrated around the same single point. So, the uncertainty about the particle's position does not disappear until the measurement is done. Instead of the particle occupying a fuzzy spread given by the wave function, it is localized into a single position. In the real world, however, the uncertainty never actually comes down to zero. This is captured by the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle, which states that the more precisely we know the position of a particle, the less we know about its momentum, and vice versa. And a very small Gaussian packet is indeed, as near as we can get to that “ideal” point. The wave function does not collapse entirely to a point, because this would mean the particle's momentum is infinitely uncertain, which would be impossible. This gives us the possibility to define the localization of the particle at a certain point by a tiny Gaussian packet, where position is certain to a reasonable degree while being matched by a certain uncertainty of its momentum. Because the Gaussian packet does not collapse down to a single point, the particle is still somewhat delocalized, but we can say with great assurance that its position is known at a high degree of precision. Is a single electron considered an actual particle in quantum mechanics, or is it always just a wave packet with definite properties at any given time? The answer, as usual, is complicated by the inherent subtleties of quantum mechanics. The reality of the situation is, to put it mildly, a bit of both. In certain contexts, we conveniently treat the electron as a point-like "particle," possessing definite characteristics like mass, charge, and spin. This is often the case when we're dealing with macroscopic phenomena or when making simple calculations. The electron, in these instances, behaves in ways we've come to expect from classical particles: colliding, interacting, and following trajectories. However, at a more fundamental level, the electron exhibits wave-like properties. It can spread out in space as a wave function, a mathematical description that dictates the probability of finding the electron at a given location. The famous "double-slit experiment" brilliantly demonstrates this duality. A stream of electrons, when fired towards a barrier with two slits, produces an interference pattern, indicative of wave behavior. A single electron doesn't simply pass through one slit or the other; it goes through both, or so it seems, somehow interfering with itself. Furthermore, the properties of the electron aren't always definite, not until a measurement is made. The wave function, representing its potential properties (position, momentum, etc.), collapses upon measurement, forcing the electron to "choose" a specific state. Before the measurement, the electron exists in a superposition of states, a blurry quantum limbo. The act of observing, of measuring, forces a "choice" to be made, imbuing the electron with definite properties. This is the essence of the observer effect, central to quantum mechanics. Thus, the electron embodies a fundamental duality. It’s both a wave and a particle, depending on the context, the scale, and the nature of the observation. It's not one or the other, but both, entwined in a bizarre, non-intuitive, and yet beautifully consistent, way. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Does quantum mechanics contradict determinism? Yes, it does. Though not in the way that is usually portrayed, which may be the root of some of the confusion. First, let me explain what determinism actually is. In physics, determinism holds that if you were to know everything at time t, then you would be able to calculate everything that happens at any t’ later time. In other words, the universe is as it is, not because of some random circumstances, but because of the way things were at the beginning. The beginning is not necessarily the Big Bang, since an adequate physical theory can always be traced to even earlier moments. But wherever things begin, at that moment, every single particle and field had some well-defined properties; and from those properties sprang everything that followed. Thus, the entire state of the universe now (and at any other moment in time) follows inexorably from the conditions that existed at the start. In this view of the world, there is no room for chance. This is in opposition to free will, where our actions are not strictly determined by prior events. Many physicists thought that such a conception of the universe was a fundamental goal of physics. As it stands today, however, quantum mechanics violates determinism. The laws of physics do not determine the future. They can at best predict the probability of finding a certain outcome, but not the outcome itself. Which means, if you were to reconstruct the state of the universe from scratch, you would never find the same state. This, however, opens up a whole can of worms. Even if the universe is not “deterministic” in the strictest scientific sense, it also does not mean that there is room for free will, or that our consciousness plays the role of some objective outside agent. At least, as far as science is concerned. Why is that? The most pressing issue is that the underlying equations are still governed by causality, which means that even if quantum mechanics is probabilistic, the future cannot influence the past. At best, the implications of this, for humanity, would be that it is not able to freely choose actions, but that those actions have arisen from conditions that we might not know. The other implication is that there is no contradiction between quantum mechanics and the so-called “many world interpretation,” or “Everettian quantum mechanics”, which holds that all possible outcomes of a quantum mechanical experiment are realized in separate universes. Does Victor Toth agree that his explanation of the cosmic microwave background with the help of pops on the square is more suitable for "substantiating" the Olbers paradox? He does. As a matter of fact, I would argue that my take on the microwave background offers a more intuitive “solution” to the Olbers paradox than the commonly accepted, and rather pedantic, explanations. The usual way of thinking about the paradox is that the universe is not infinite, and the finite amount of time that has passed since the beginning of the universe limits the amount of light that can reach us, which in turn resolves the conflict: At any given point, on average, light emitted by a distant star simply has not had enough time to reach us. But I think this begs the question. Since the universe is said to be expanding, and because the speed of light is finite, it does follow that the light emitted at the beginning of the universe, from a point source, would be reaching us right now. Fine. But that means the light from the rest of the universe wouldn’t (yet) reach us. So, given that the universe is so very old, why aren’t we constantly being bombarded by light from every direction? The answer is, in its current form, the Olbers paradox is flawed. One must account for the expansion of the universe. The expansion, according to the current best cosmological models, is accelerating. Therefore, the distance to any given light source changes over time, and so do the light wavelengths. What is m in f=ma, rest mass, inertial mass, variable mass, or gravitational mass? It turns out that the “m” in the equation f = ma is a rather subtle beast. First of all: what is "a" in the equation f = ma? Well, it’s that property of an object's motion which we call “acceleration”. I.e., the change in that object’s velocity with time. In classical mechanics, it’s always a well-defined quantity. In special and general relativity, however… it’s not quite the same thing. But we shall leave that for now. Then, “f” is “force”. Force, in Newtonian physics, is some push or pull, and it causes an object to accelerate. But what is “m”? Well, as it turns out, it depends on what you are talking about. First and foremost, it is the "inertial mass." Which is to say, “m” is the measure of the resistance of an object to acceleration. The more massive some object is, the harder it is to accelerate it. It’s as simple as that. Therefore, in classical mechanics, there is only one type of mass: the inertial mass. However, as soon as one introduces Newton’s law of gravity, it becomes apparent that there is also “gravitational mass”. That’s the measure of how strongly an object is affected by gravity. Now: in Newtonian gravity, the inertial mass and the gravitational mass are exactly the same thing. You could write two entirely different equations: f = ma for the effects of an applied force and f_g = G M m / r² for gravity. Here, G is the gravitational constant; M is the mass of the object doing the attracting; m is the “gravitational mass” of the attracted object; and r is the distance between them. In this case, the “m” in f_g = G M m / r² **is** the gravitational mass. Only if you assume that the inertial and gravitational masses are equal, can you simplify these two equations into something like g = G M / r² , for instance. As it turns out, there is no known reason why these two masses should be exactly the same. We have only a vast amount of experimental evidence proving, to a high degree of precision, that they are. Then what is “rest mass”? In Special Relativity, the "m" in f = ma is *not* the same. It is the so-called "relativistic mass", which depends on the object's relativistic speed. But if we are dealing with an object that is at rest relative to the observer, the relativistic mass collapses to the "rest mass", which is the equivalent of “m” in classical mechanics. This also implies that energy and rest mass are equivalent, as in Einstein’s famous E = mc². So, is “m” variable? Yes and no. In classical mechanics, “m” **is** a variable, as both gravity and acceleration depend on the amount of this variable. But in Special Relativity, it is also implied that m, relativistic mass, is also a function of the speed of the object. However, the answer is “no” if this variable is the rest mass. But the difference between the two is essentially semantic: in both cases, we are talking about the same variable of mass. As opposed to the gravitational mass, the inertial mass, and all the other masses; but still, the same variable. By the way, I find it fascinating that the unit for both the inertial mass and gravitational mass is the same: kg. But, then again, I’m a physicist. Why a free isolated electon cant fully absorb a photon? Because you cannot destroy momentum. This is a fundamental principle, like conservation of energy. But let's rewind for a bit and discuss what photons are. You may think they are like little bullets. After all, in many ways that's exactly what they are: Photons have momentum, and they can impart that momentum to other particles upon interaction. However, the analogy with bullets breaks down when one accounts for what really makes a photon *a photon*. It turns out, a photon's momentum is not only equal to its energy divided by the speed of light (p = E / c), but also that **it *must* travel at the speed of light**. This is non-negotiable. You cannot catch a photon, you cannot slow it down, and you cannot make it stop. So, if an electron, initially at rest, were to absorb a photon, then the photon would be gone. In its place would be an electron. By conservation of energy the electron would have to gain the energy carried by the photon. Also, that energy would increase the electron’s inertial mass. And here’s the crux: The electron would now have non-zero energy and a non-zero mass, but it would have zero momentum. This is simply impossible, but consistent with the laws of physics. Indeed, this is what we mean when we say that an interaction "violates" the laws of physics. So, you may be thinking you can get rid of the problem by giving the electron some momentum. But let’s try that out anyway. The electron gains energy and momentum, not enough to just absorb that photon: a new particle, or maybe another electron, must also be created to carry away that extra momentum. This is where the “virtual particles” come in. Such processes are possible within the rules of quantum field theory, but only if the additional “intermediate” particles can only be created and annihilated very quickly, due to Heisenberg's uncertainty principle. But even that is not the answer. Not yet, at least. If an electron *does* interact with a photon, it has to change its momentum, but that momentum has to be absorbed. So even that is not a complete answer. But it is, nevertheless, correct. Perhaps you could view that “interaction” as an intermediate step on the way of the electron’s path after the moment it absorbs the photon. In fact, in many such cases, the photon has to *scatter* with the electron rather than absorb into it; then the electron has a different direction of motion. So the short answer to your very good question is the following: the electron cannot fully absorb the photon because they would then violate the conservation of momentum. Is it fair to say that there is the equivalent of infinite acceleration at the event horizon of a black hole? No, it's not fair. Acceleration (that which, when integrated over time, gives velocity), while very, very large near the event horizon, is not infinite. But there is a point where time, as experienced by an outside observer, appears to stop. We can quantify this by looking at the “coordinate time” which is used to make the mathematical models which describe black holes. If you are an outside observer, watching an object fall into a black hole, you would see their progress slow down more and more the closer they get to the event horizon. They would approach the horizon asymptotically, i.e., in principle, never reaching it. In fact, an outside observer would never see anything fall into the black hole at all. But if spacetime is warped in such a way that an outside observer would never watch an object cross the event horizon, why does the event horizon exist at all? Because an object falling into the black hole *does* cross the event horizon from their own perspective. You simply can't know what happens inside the event horizon from the outside. To determine what happens inside, you would need to cross the event horizon yourself. Even from the perspective of this hapless traveler, the object doesn’t experience infinite acceleration itself. What happens to the object is that, as it falls into the black hole, it gets stretched and squeezed by the tidal forces. These tidal forces, arising from the extreme gravitational gradient, become increasingly powerful as the object approaches the singularity at the center of the black hole. It is here, at the singularity, where “infinite” effects begin to take place… But as for the “event horizon”, the object merely experiences a rather bumpy ride.

If all of the mass energy of colliding black holes is contained within their event horizons, how does the collision release any energy? Then, they come together. When they touch, the event horizons merge, and a single, larger event horizon forms. The energy released is the difference between the combined mass-energy before the collision, and the mass-energy contained in the new, single black hole. But what about the escaping energy? Where does that originate? The answer lies in the gravitational waves. These are ripples in spacetime. These waves emanate from the rapidly changing gravitational field during the collision, carrying away energy. The energy released in gravitational waves is not associated with the mass-energy that remains trapped inside the new, larger black hole. It’s a byproduct, a sort of “excess”, of the violent cosmic merger. The gravitational waves carry the "information" about the collision, the location and trajectories of the initial black holes and the geometry of the resulting fusion. They emanate outwards, away from the new event horizon, and they don’t get “stuck” inside. Thus, none of the mass-energy is escaping from the event horizon by itself. It is the changing gravitational field, induced by the merger of the two, that carries the released energy in the form of those gravitational waves. Any such radiation would be quickly absorbed into the new black hole. Furthermore, any radiation that may get ejected would in fact be captured inside, or at least at the horizon. This concept underscores the nature of black holes: All mass-energy remains trapped. Only energy associated with the distortion of spacetime itself can escape. How do quarks give rise to the mass of protons and neutrons? Mass is a peculiar thing. At least in the context of subatomic particles. You see, most of the mass of ordinary matter comes from protons and neutrons, which in turn are made of quarks. But a quark itself, the fundamental constituent, only has a very small mass. This is especially true for the up and down quarks (the kind that mostly make up regular matter): their mass is negligible compared to the mass of a proton or a neutron. So where does the mass come from? Well, it's a bit of a sleight of hand, really. The seemingly simple answer is that the majority of mass comes from the energy associated with the "glue" that holds everything together: the strong force, carried by the gluons that bind the quarks. That's the oversimplified, yet useful, explanation. Even more precisely, the proton or the neutron are not simply three quarks bouncing around. They're three quarks, a sea of virtual quarks and antiquarks, and a lot of gluons exchanging energy and momentum. But their total energy and momentum are not exactly equal to the mass of the proton or neutron. This is where the infamous “quantum effects” come into play. You know, the ones that the quantum gravity theorists are banging their heads against the wall to find a sensible explanation for. (Although really, most of what's done nowadays is to apply numerical simulation.) But that’s as far as it can go, because any deeper explanation requires going through a lot of rather advanced math. However, a good “rule of thumb” would be as follows: If you want to consider the mass of a particle, and its internal structure, you need to know the energy density of its constituents. That is the first fundamental ingredient. You also need to account for the pressure those constituents exert. (Remember what a perfect fluid is?) The pressure on each constituent arises from their interactions, and from their confinement. You also need some kind of external force to keep everything together. This is provided by the strong force that acts between the quarks. It’s not the same as gravity (as many confused people may think), so don’t get them mixed up. But in the end, calculating this correctly calls for an extremely complicated mathematical description: Quantum Chromodynamics, or QCD. Which can only be solved by brute force: numerical simulations, essentially. But the basic concept is this: The mass of a proton (or a neutron) is not the sum of the masses of its parts. It is, instead, the sum of their energy and internal pressure. The larger the pressure, the larger the mass. And as a matter of fact, the vast majority of mass comes from that pressure. Brian Greene said: “as particles … try to move through space, they have to burrow through the Higgs field, and that is what gives them mass”. Does that mean that particles that keep at rest in the frame of the Higgs fied are gravitationally massless? No, not quite. The Higgs field gives particles their mass by interacting with them, but this interaction does not negate the effects of gravity. The mass of a particle is what couples it to gravity in the first place. Think about it this way: the Higgs field is a ubiquitous medium permeating all of space. Any particle, irrespective of its state of motion within the Higgs field, is subject to this field’s influence, which determines its mass. This mass, in turn, dictates how the particle responds to the gravitational field. Furthermore, particles don’t “keep at rest” in the frame of the Higgs field. Even if they did, the gravitational effects would still be there. Gravity, unlike the concept of mass derived from the Higgs field, is tied to the overall energy-momentum of a system, and this energy-momentum will always be “felt” in the presence of a gravitational field. So no, whether a particle is moving relative to the Higgs field or not is irrelevant to its gravitational mass as long as it has mass. The Higgs field is thus not a substitute for gravity, nor does it obviate its effects. In the end, mass determined by the Higgs field is a prerequisite to feeling gravity in the first place.

How does a black hole destroy matter but not light? Excellent question, a deceptively simple one at that. The thing is, a black hole does not *destroy* matter. It merely changes its relationship with the rest of the universe. The gravitational field of a black hole is characterized by such a steep gradient that at a certain distance from it – the event horizon – it becomes inescapable. (If you knew the escape velocity of an object from a certain gravitational field, you would know how fast you would need to accelerate to overcome the effects of the pulling force.) Now, light, too, has to, in effect, “escape”. The escape velocity is what it takes to overcome the effective “pull” of gravity. As you probably already know, the speed of light is the ultimate speed limit of the universe; no object can move faster, and that includes the things that make up light itself (photons). But at the event horizon, the escape velocity is precisely the speed of light. Inside the event horizon, the escape velocity is greater than the speed of light. No matter what, something inside its event horizon will not be able to leave. It’s a one-way street. That includes not only material objects but also the light they might emit. So it’s not that the black hole “destroys” the stuff, but that stuff simply cannot go anywhere else. It gets “frozen” on the event horizon, as an outside observer would see it (a phenomenon known as “gravitational time dilation”, but that's another story). Eventually, the fate of the captured matter would amount to the central singularity. But that is not true destruction, either: it's not some kind of cosmic grinding machine. How is the speed of gravity determined? The speed of gravity, as it turns out, is the speed of light. However, I must immediately clarify that this is not a self-evident fact. Indeed, if you were to ask me the question a century ago, I would have probably answered that there is no such thing as the "speed of gravity." Before Einstein, the predominant view of gravity was the Newtonian view: gravity is an instantaneous phenomenon that acts at a distance. The Sun, for instance, exerts an immediate gravitational influence on the Earth, tugging on it even from the enormous distance between them. Likewise, the Earth exerts an instantaneous influence on us. This is not an unreasonable explanation. It works, in fact, to a very high level of accuracy. But it isn't right. Einstein's theory of gravity, the General Theory of Relativity, changed that. In Einstein's theory, gravity is not a force at all, but a consequence of the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy. Furthermore, changes in the gravitational field, like any other field, can only propagate at a finite speed. What speed? The speed of light. It may not be obvious, but it is the only reasonable speed. Consider, for instance, that if gravity traveled at a speed greater than the speed of light, causality would be violated, as cause and effect would be reversed. The speed of gravity is, of course, a matter of physics, not philosophy. Therefore, it is something that can be measured with experiments. But which experiments? That's the cool part: It took a while. At first, the effects were so minuscule that they couldn't be detected. Furthermore, what is to be measured? It took decades before physicists came up with clever experiments that could measure the speed of gravity, i.e., the speed at which gravitational perturbations propagate from one point in space to another. In the end, it was measured in two separate types of experiments: gravitational waves and the deflection of light. The detection of gravitational waves is the most direct method. Gravitational waves are ripples in spacetime caused by accelerating massive objects, and they travel at the speed of light. In 2017, the LIGO and Virgo collaborations detected gravitational waves from the merger of two neutron stars. These waves arrived at Earth at precisely the same time as a burst of light from the same location. This result provided strong evidence that gravity travels at the speed of light. Furthermore, the precise measurement of the deflection of light when it passes near a massive object, like the Sun, also provides compelling evidence that gravity travels at the speed of light. Any change in the Sun's position, then, would result in a corresponding change in how light is deflected after a delay. Again, the delay time turned out to be the same as the light travel time. These two types of experiments, each employing different methods, have confirmed that the speed of gravity is indeed the speed of light. How can virtual particles become real particles e.g. while Hawking radiation? This is a question that even seasoned physicists grapple with, and the answer, as with many inquiries at the quantum level, is not entirely straightforward. One must first understand the fundamental nature of virtual particles: they are, essentially, fleeting disturbances, momentary excursions from the established laws of energy conservation. They exist only briefly, popping into and out of existence so quickly that they evade direct detection. Yet, despite their ephemeral nature, these virtual particles play a crucial role in mediating interactions, providing the "glue" that holds the universe together. They are, in a sense, the building blocks of nothing. Hawking radiation, a concept arising from the intersection of general relativity and quantum mechanics, offers a particularly intriguing scenario where these virtual entities undergo a remarkable transformation. Imagine a black hole, a region of spacetime where gravity is so intense that nothing, not even light, can escape. Near the event horizon, the boundary beyond which escape is impossible, quantum effects become pronounced. Virtual particle pairs, constantly spawning and annihilating, are created. But the reason it's not *always* conserved in relativistic situations is because “mass” is, in a sense, a derived quantity from E and p, but most importantly, it is a consequence of the interactions of the system particles within the rest of the system. Einstein’s general relativity reframes the narrative. Gravity isn't a force at all; instead, it's the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy. Objects then move along the curves of this spacetime, which give the illusion of being acted upon by gravity. Furthermore, the effects propagate at the speed of light. Thus, Newton's views, predicated on classical mechanics, are an approximation of Einstein's view. Einstein's theory is more precise, accounting for scenarios where gravity is extremely strong or where the speed of light is relevant, while Newton’s is useful in situations, i.e. those involving relatively low gravity. When it comes to quantum mechanics, though, things get trickier. Quantum mechanics is a description of the behavior of matter and energy at the atomic and subatomic levels. It is based on a set of principles that are fundamentally at odds with Einstein's. The quantum world is discrete, probabilistic, and subject to the observer effect, while the world of general relativity is smooth, deterministic, and independent of the observer. Reconciling these two theories is one of the greatest open problems in physics. So, to answer the question, yes, there are incompatibilities, but the nuances depend on the particular perspective. Einstein's physics built upon – and improved – Newton’s, while quantum theory poses a more profound challenge. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Can anything emerge in space other than mass and energy to be equivalent and convertible to mass or energy? If it can then how will we write E=mc2? That’s an interesting question. The short answer is no, nothing else “emerges” from space beyond mass and energy, which, according to the most celebrated equation of physics E=mc², are indeed equivalent and, as we all know, freely convertible to each other. Now, what *exactly* do we mean when we say “emerge”? It’s not a precisely defined term, but let’s begin with a classic example: What “emerges” when you drop a ball? A physicist will tell you that, in the vast emptiness of intergalactic space, the ball itself, and all that surrounds it, are composed of fields. The ball is nothing but a concentrated excitation in these fields. These are fundamental fields, which includes the Higgs field, the electromagnetic field, and so forth. But that drop… even this simple phenomenon becomes very complicated. After all, gravity is also involved. The Earth's gravitational field interacts with the ball, causing it to fall. And, of course, there is the entire quantum realm. The ball is composed of countless subatomic particles, each with a wave-like nature. So the trajectory of the ball is not simply the result of a single force, but rather the complex interplay of many different forces and fields. Then, we also need to define, what is this “space” itself? Space is not some empty canvas upon which everything else is painted. It is a physical entity, also subject to the influence of everything within it. The very fabric of spacetime can be stretched and curved by the presence of energy and mass. All these interactions give rise to a multitude of “emergent” properties: momentum, the way the ball spins, etc. However, these emergent properties, that are subject to be measured, still boil down to a combination of the fundamental fields, described by the equation E=mc². Why does general relativity predict that the wavelength of light will be shifted due to the galaxies mass in an effect called gravitational redshift? Because general relativity is a geometrical theory of gravitation, and light, like everything else, follows the curvature of the spacetime, which in turn is determined by the distribution of mass & energy, as encoded in the Einstein field equations. In the simplest terms, the presence of a massive object like a galaxy creates a “gravitational well” around it, and the light waves that try to “climb out” of this well have to expend part of their energy. Since the energy carried by a light wave is proportional to its frequency, a loss of energy implies a loss of frequency, which, since the speed of light is constant, implies an increase in the wavelength. That’s the redshift: the wavelength has been stretched out, shifted toward the red end of the electromagnetic spectrum. The amount of the shift depends on the mass of the object and the distance from the object’s center, and, of course, on the wavelength of the light itself. The more massive an object, the greater the shift; the closer the light source is to the object, the greater the shift; and the shorter the wavelength, the greater the shift. This effect has been experimentally verified many times and is one of the key pieces of evidence that supports general relativity. But it’s not just that the wavelength is shifted. The duration of time, as measured by an observer at a different gravitational potential, will also seem to change. Take a light source on the surface of a white dwarf. For the light source, time is passing normally. But for an observer far away, time on the surface of the white dwarf is passing at a slower rate. This means that the light waves emitted by the white dwarf will not only be redshifted but will also arrive at the observer at a slower rate. The effect is so minute that it's imperceptible to the naked eye, and even by many instruments. But with today’s modern instruments, it can be measured and the experimental measurement once again matches the theoretical prediction with impressive precision. Why does the weakness of gravity prevent scientists from finding the graviton? Well, first off, let's nail down what the graviton *is*. The graviton is the hypothetical, as-yet-undetectable, fundamental particle that mediates the force of gravity. In the same way that photons are the gauge bosons of the electromagnetic force, and gluons are the gauge bosons of the strong nuclear force, the graviton is supposed to be the gauge boson of gravity. The Standard Model of particle physics, the most successful scientific theory ever created, explains only the electromagnetic, weak, and strong forces. It doesn't account for gravity at all. The problem is that, at the quantum scale, gravity is incredibly, almost ridiculously, weak. This is why we have yet to identify the graviton. The math works, in a way, but the numbers are minuscule. Let's put it this way: the gravitational force between two protons is about 10^36 times smaller than the electromagnetic force. That's not just a large number, but a *vast* number. In the subatomic world, it's as if gravity barely even *exists*. This extreme weakness is why we haven't directly observed gravitons and, furthermore, why the quantum theory of gravity is proving so difficult to formulate. We can't simply scale up experiments, either. Even the largest black holes, from a quantum perspective, are still pretty small. The gravitational effects are strong but the effects of gravity on spacetime are, from a quantum point of view, so weak that they would be lost in all the rest of the “noise” in the Universe. Furthermore, it's even harder to detect something that doesn't interact very much with matter. Photons, for instance, readily interact with electrically charged particles and, for this reason, photons are easy to find. However, the gravitational interaction is so weak that the graviton interaction with matter would also be remarkably weak, with most gravitons passing right through anything, without leaving much of a trace. The few gravitons that do interact would be lost in a sea of background. Then, there are a few other issues, such as the fact that gravitons, if they exist, would almost certainly have zero mass, meaning they should travel at the speed of light, similar to photons. This makes detection even harder. So, to summarize: The extreme weakness of gravity, relative to the other forces, combined with the graviton's very weak interactions, makes the detection of gravitons exceptionally difficult. Was the German mathematician Hilbert's final derivation of the general relativity found to contain a key error by subsequent peer scholars? So Einstein is still regarded as the first person to publish the correct equations of general relativity? As I understand it, Hilbert indeed submitted his equations to the journal *Annalen der Physik* a few days before Einstein. But Einstein's work was completed independently and was later published. Both papers presented the same field equations, which describe how gravity is produced by mass and energy that also predict the bending of light, gravitational time dilation, and other phenomena. Therefore, the answer is yes, Einstein is still regarded as the first scientist to publish the correct equations of general relativity. And the mathematics are correct, although there’s a philosophical difference between both: Einstein’s theory offers a description of gravity as a curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy. The initial calculations were based entirely on physical argument, and every subsequent physical prediction has been verified by observation. Hilbert’s approach was from a mathematical rather than a physical viewpoint, which is why he never followed up with the actual predictions. What is the propagator for a massless scalar field, and how can you compute it using C++? Ah, the massless scalar field; a staple of quantum field theory, and the backbone of almost all other fields. Its propagator, a deceptively simple object (until, of course, you crack the equations open), serves as the bridge between the quantum field and the classical, observable world. It’s a mathematical construct that calculates the probability amplitude of a particle (or, rather, a disturbance in the field) moving from one point in spacetime to another. Think of it as the fundamental “building block” for all interactions mediated by this particular field. Its form is elegantly simple: D(x - y) = ∫ [d^4 k / (2π)^4] * [i / k^2] * e^(-i k⋅(x - y)). Here, x and y represent two points in spacetime, and the integral is over all possible four-momenta, *k*. The term *k^2* (k-squared) is a shorthand for k_0^2 - k_1^2 - k_2^2 - k_3^2 , where k_0 is the energy component of the four-momentum, and k_1, k_2, and k_3 are the spatial components. The "i" term in the numerator? That's just a quirk of relativistic quantum field theory. C++? Ah, yes, the programmer's favorite tool. You will need some libraries, such as `cmath, complex, and numerical_integration` (if you don’t want to write your own numerical integration algorithms). First off, define a class or a struct to represent four-vectors (four-momenta and spacetime coordinates): `struct FourVector { double t, x, y, z; };`. Then, we need a function to calculate the dot product. Given the dot product, we can define a function to calculate k^2: `double k_squared(FourVector k) { return k.t*k.t - k.x*k.x - k.y*k.y - k.z*k.z; }`. Here’s a simple C++ function implementing the propagator:```c++#include <iostream>#include <cmath>#include <complex>#include <numbers>using namespace std;struct FourVector { double t, x, y, z; };double dot_product(FourVector k, FourVector delta_x) {    return k.t * delta_x.t - k.x * delta_x.x - k.y * delta_x.y - k.z * delta_x.z;}double k_squared(FourVector k) {    return k.t*k.t - k.x*k.x - k.y*k.y - k.z*k.z;}complex<double> propagator(FourVector x, FourVector y, double k_max) {    FourVector delta_x = {x.t - y.t, x.x - y.x, x.y - y.y, x.z - y.z};    complex<double> integral_result = 0.0;    // Approximate Numerical Integration (4D)    int num_points = 100; // Reduce if compiling takes too long    for (int i = 0; i < num_points; ++i) {        double kt = k_max * (2.0 * i / num_points - 1.0); // -k_max to k_max        for (int j = 0; j < num_points; ++j) {            double kx = k_max * (2.0 * j / num_points - 1.0);            for (int l = 0; l < num_points; ++l) {                double ky = k_max * (2.0 * l / num_points - 1.0);                for (int m = 0; m < num_points; ++m) {                    double kz = k_max * (2.0 * m / num_points - 1.0);                    FourVector k = {kt, kx, ky, kz};                    double k_sq = k_squared(k);                    if (abs(k_sq) < 1e-6) continue;  // Avoid singularity                    complex<double> integrand = (1.0+0.0i) / (k_sq) * std::exp(-1.0i * dot_product(k, delta_x));                    integral_result += integrand;                }            }        }    }    integral_result*= 1.0/pow(2.0*std::numbers::pi, 4)*pow(2*k_max, 4)/pow(num_points, 4);    return integral_result;}int main() {    FourVector x = {1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0}; // Example spacetime point    FourVector y = {0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0}; // Another spacetime point    double k_max = 20.0; // Integration cut-off    complex<double> result = propagator(x, y, k_max);    cout.precision(4);    cout << "Propagator at (x, y): " << fixed << result << endl;    return 0;}```I've included a simple if statement to skip the zero-valued points in the loop. Be warned that the four-dimensional integration is quite computationally expensive. You may want to reduce the number of points evaluated in the integral, or find ways to optimize or parallelize the code. More sophisticated numerical integration techniques (e.g., Monte Carlo methods) could be significantly more efficient for these types of integrals. Another consideration is the "infrared divergence," arising from the fact that the propagator’s integrand has no characteristic scale. This is why *k_max* is needed. Does the existence of Hawking radiation suggest that nothing truly enters a black hole? Not exactly. The thing about Hawking radiation is that it is not emitted by anything that ever *was* inside the black hole. Rather, it's a radiation that originates just outside the event horizon, as a consequence of quantum mechanical effects. In other words, the black hole itself gives rise to this radiation, not something that got “sucked in”. The best way to put it is that the singularity (which, after all, is a singularity) does not simply consume anything. It’s difficult to visualize, I admit, but the only thing that a “black hole” truly absorbs is the information about what it was made of. A black hole’s mass, charge, and angular momentum define its exterior spacetime, and this is all that matters. Otherwise, the black hole “remembers” nothing, a principle known as "no hair theorem.” Consider this: You’re hovering very close to the event horizon. You observe a quantum fluctuation. A particle-antiparticle pair pops into existence, and because of the extreme gravitational field, one of those, say the particle, falls in, and its antiparticle escapes. It’s as if the black hole “borrowed” this antiparticle, emitting it as Hawking radiation, and the process costs the black hole the energy equivalent to the particle. Thus, the black hole “loses” mass. Now this process is repeated ad nauseam. The black hole shrinks, eventually evaporating. If the black hole were formed by the collapse of a star, then, in the end, all that remains of the star is…. nothing. The black hole has lost all of the information about the star’s composition. This is, in a nutshell, the information paradox. However – and this is an important “however” – nothing in this process suggests information is truly destroyed. So the jury is still out. There may be a way to retrieve this information, something the quantum gravity theorists keep working on. If we ever come up with a solid theory of quantum gravity, we may have definitive answers. What would happen if something went through a black hole? Well, the short answer is, we don’t know. The longer answer is that if general relativity is correct, the event horizon is a one-way street. Anything that falls into it, stays in it. And whatever is inside, is doomed. But doomed to what? Well, that’s the real problem: what happens inside a black hole is beyond our current understanding of physics. We can only guess. According to classical general relativity, the interior of a black hole contains a singularity, a point of infinite density. But we know that general relativity is not the whole story: it may work perfectly well for describing the trajectories of planets or the distortion of spacetime around massive objects, but it’s fundamentally incomplete. It does not play well with quantum mechanics, and thus it can’t tell us what really happens at very high concentrations of energy. So what can we say? Well, here is what we *think* we know. Let’s start with the simplest case: a black hole that has been around forever, with nothing falling into it, and no quantum effects to speak of. Such a black hole is defined solely by its mass, its charge, and its angular momentum. And according to the no-hair theorem, that is all that can be known about it. In this case, we would expect that whatever falls in, would eventually reach the singularity. And as the singularity is approached, tidal forces would increase without bound. So our hapless traveler, after crossing the event horizon, would be “spaghettified” into oblivion. That’s it. But… the caveat is that this may never happen. The simplest calculations show that black holes are not forever: they emit Hawking radiation and eventually evaporate, which turns them, at least in this simplistic picture, into an unstable object that simply vanishes in a puff of photons and other particles. If that’s the case, then what “goes through” is not what you might expect. But… we do not actually know. The math is very hard, and the experiments are impossible.
